newsitem.title: BELGIUM: BELGIUM TO LET SOME SOLDIERS WORK FOUR-DAY WEEK.
newsitem.headline: BELGIUM TO LET SOME SOLDIERS WORK FOUR-DAY WEEK.

text.p: Members of Belgium's armed forces will gain the right to work part time under measures to encourage older staff to leave, the government announced on Friday.
Defence Minister Jean-Pol Poncelet said, however, that front-line troops would be excluded under an executive order signed by King Albert.

Belgium has some 500 troops stationed on Zaire's border waiting to evacuate Belgian nationals should that country's civil war spread. It has around 1,300 more on duty with United Nations and NATO forces in Croatia and Bosnia.
"Nobody wants or expects our paratroops in Brazzaville (Congo) to be doing a four-day week," Poncelet told a news conference after the weekly cabinet meeting.

Poncelet said that in practice around half the armed forces would be affected by the measures, which offer them the option to work a four-day week, take early retirement or go on career breaks lasting up to five years.

The measures, he said, were designed to speed up the departure of older staff from the armed forces, thereby meeting defence cut targets announced in 1992, as well as to create room for younger recruits.
Older staff could be obliged to accept early retirement from 1998 if not enough had left by then, he said.

Belgium's military currently employs around 1,000 more officers and servicemen than projected under the 1992 plan, which aimed to cut the size of the services from 54,800 to 47,500 by the end of 1997.

The original plan -- which included a freeze on defence spending until 1998 and the sell-off of ships, tanks, planes and other weapons systems -- was criticised at the time by some of Belgium's NATO allies.
Poncelet said he expected no such reaction this time, noting that many other NATO countries had followed Belgium's lead in announcing defence cuts following the end of the Cold War.
"This time we are introducing part-time work in a limited way. I think in the years ahead others will do the same thing," Poncelet said.

"The measures will help us rejuvenate our forces, which our (NATO) partners have asked, and also create room for new spending within our defence budget, which they also want," he added. REUTER 281727 GMT mar 97
